content: 1. Limited removal processes are those that achieve less than 80% removal of contaminants. 2. Processes achieving approximately 80% or more removal are considered highly effective. 3. For the most effective treatment methods, the concentration of the chemical (measured in mg/L) that should be achievable is indicated. 4. Some processes might be effective but are less likely to be applied due to cost considerations. 5. Treatment performance for cyanobacterial cells and cyanotoxins is evaluated based on established guideline or reference values. 6. Chlorination, coagulation, activated carbon, ozonation, advanced oxidation, membranes, and sediment passage are common treatment methods for cyanobacterial cells and cyanotoxins. 7. Chlorination, ozonation, or advanced oxidation may release cyanotoxins during the treatment process. 8. A removal efficiency of 80% or more is denoted as highly effective. 9. Only chemicals with available treatment data are included in the evaluation. 10. A blank entry in the evaluation table indicates either complete ineffectiveness of the process or lack of data on its effectiveness. 11. Sediment passage includes slow sand filtration and bank filtration, which can also be effective in removing cyanobacteria and cyanotoxins. 12. Percolation through soils, such as during artificial groundwater recharge, can effectively remove cyanobacteria and cyanotoxins. 13. Some processes are not effective for anatoxins. 14. Membrane effectiveness depends on pore size and the specific toxin being targeted. 15. Newly installed cement materials can leach lime, increasing pH, alkalinity, and hardness in water. 16. Cement contains various metals that may leach into water. 17. Cement's susceptibility to aggressive ions like chloride or sulfate can lead to structural failure. 18. The aggressivity index is used to assess the potential for concrete dissolution. 19. A pH of 5 or higher may be necessary to control cement corrosion. 20. Copper corrosion in pipework and hot water cylinders can cause blue water, staining, and taste issues. 21. Copper tubing is prone to general corrosion, impingement attack, and pitting corrosion. 22. Soft water with low pH and high temperature exacerbates impingement attack. 23. Pitting corrosion in copper is associated with hard groundwater containing high carbon dioxide and dissolved oxygen. 24. Phosphates are used to suppress copper corrosion in some cases. 25. Surface waters with organic color may also contribute to pitting corrosion. 26. Copper pipes can fail due to localized pitting corrosion, leading to perforations with minimal metal loss. 27. Type I pitting affects cold water systems (below 40°C) and is linked to hard borehole waters and carbon films from manufacturing. 28. Type II pitting occurs in hot water systems (above 60°C) and is associated with soft waters. 29. New pipes without a protective oxide layer are more prone to general and pitting corrosion. 30. Calcium carbonate precipitation indices like Langelier and Ryznar are not reliable predictors of copper corrosion. 31. Iron corrosion in water distribution systems can lead to red water due to excessive corrosion of iron pipes. 32. Iron corrosion involves oxidation of the metal, typically by dissolved oxygen, forming iron(III) precipitates. 33. Tubercules form on pipe surfaces as a result of iron corrosion. 34. pH and alkalinity are key factors in determining whether the precipitate forms a protective scale. 35. Calcium, chloride, and sulfate concentrations also influence iron corrosion. 36. Successful iron corrosion control involves adjusting pH, hardness, and alkalinity to specific levels. 37. Silicates and polyphosphates are often described as corrosion inhibitors but may only mask corrosion effects rather than prevent it. 38. Lead corrosion (plumbosolvency) is a significant concern, especially in older homes with lead piping or lead-based solder. 39. Galvanized iron pipes can accumulate incoming lead and release it later as particulates. 40. Lead solubility is governed by the formation of lead carbonates as pipe deposits. 41. Wherever possible, lead pipework should be replaced. 42. Orthophosphate and other phosphates are effective in suppressing lead dissolution. 43. Lead concentrations increase with longer water stagnation times in lead pipes. 44. Flushing pipework before drawing water for consumption can reduce lead exposure. 45. Galvanic corrosion occurs when lead is coupled with copper, accelerating lead corrosion. 46. The rate of galvanic corrosion is influenced by chloride concentration. 47. Zinc dosing with orthophosphate and pH adjustment can reduce galvanic corrosion. 48. Nickel in water may leach from nickelor chromium-plated taps and stainless steel pipes. 49. Nickel leaching is influenced by stagnation time and can be reduced by pH control. 50. Consumers, especially nickel-sensitive individuals, should flush nickelor chromium-plated taps before use. 51. Galvanized pipes release zinc and may also leach cadmium and lead. 52. Zinc solubility in water depends on pH and total inorganic carbon concentrations. 53. Protective deposits of basic zinc carbonate form over time but may not develop in soft waters with low alkalinity. 54. Galvanized steel is unsuitable for waters with high carbon dioxide concentrations or low alkalinity. 55. Electrolytic corrosion can occur when galvanized steel or iron pipes are connected to copper or brass fittings. 56. Guidance levels for radionuclides in drinking water are rounded to the nearest order of magnitude. 57. Analytical methods and treatment technologies for radionuclides are detailed in various international standards and publications.
